claims.claim: The difficulty of guessing a password grows exponentially with its length because each added character multiplies the search space, so length contributes to strength far more than added symbols or character-type mixing.
NIST SP 800-63B Revision 4 was finalized on August 26, 2025, and governs how systems ('verifiers') should handle passwords, which it calls memorized secrets.

NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires a minimum of 15 characters for a password used as a single authentication factor (SHALL), permits a minimum of 8 characters when the password is only part of multi-factor authentication, and requires systems to permit a maximum of at least 64 characters (SHOULD).
NIST SP 800-63B-4 states verifiers SHALL NOT require periodic password changes and shall force a change only when there is evidence of compromise.
NIST SP 800-63B-4 prohibits imposing composition rules (e.g., required mixtures of character types) on passwords.

NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires verifiers to screen prospective passwords against a blocklist of values known to be commonly used, expected, or compromised (e.g., from prior breach corpuses) and to reject matches.
NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires verifiers to allow password managers and autofill and to permit pasting into the password field.

The current guidance reverses long-standing advice (forced periodic rotation and mandatory composition rules) because both were found to make passwords weaker in practice: rotation encourages predictable minor edits and composition rules produce predictable patterns.

Reusing a password across sites is dangerous because a breach of one site exposes credentials that attackers replay against other sites in an automated credential-stuffing attack; because the credentials are real, no cracking is required.

A password manager generates, encrypts, stores, and autofills a unique strong password for each account so the user need remember only one master password; CISA recommends using one and summarizes strong passwords as long (at least 16 characters), random, and unique, or a passphrase of four to seven unrelated words.
A password alone is not sufficient protection for important accounts because any single secret can be phished or leaked; multifactor authentication is recommended as an additional layer.

Illustrative entropy: a random 8-character password from ~95 printable characters is about 95^8 (~6.6x10^15, ~53 bits); a random 5-word passphrase from a 7,776-word list is about 7,776^5 (~2.8x10^19, ~65 bits), thousands of times larger.

conflictingEvidence.issue: NIST's mandatory minimum (15 characters single-factor) versus CISA's consumer recommendation (at least 16 characters).
positions: NIST SP 800-63B-4 SHALL require 15 characters minimum for single-factor passwords
CISA consumer guidance recommends at least 16 characters, longer is stronger
conflictingEvidence.resolution: These are consistent in direction (favor length); the small numeric difference reflects a mandatory floor for systems (NIST) versus a consumer rule of thumb (CISA). The lesson presents both accurately and does not treat either number as the only correct value.

unsupportedExistingClaims: Generated draft boilerplate was treated as editorial intent only and not used as evidence; any specific claims it contained were re-derived from primary sources or discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Ensured the lesson states the CURRENT NIST position (no forced rotation, no composition rules, breach screening) and explicitly flags that this reversed the older 'change every 90 days / require symbols' advice, rather than repeating the outdated guidance.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management (Revision 4)
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), U.S. Department of Commerce
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative U.S. standards publication, Revision 4 finalized August 26, 2025 (read via WebFetch of the official HTML at pages.nist.gov/800-63-4). Supports the memorized-secret (password) requirements used in the lesson: SHALL require 15-character minimum for single-factor passwords and 8-character minimum when used only within MFA; SHOULD permit a maximum of at least 64 characters; SHALL NOT require periodic password changes and force change only on evidence of compromise; SHALL NOT impose composition rules; SHALL screen prospective passwords against a blocklist of commonly used, expected, or compromised values (e.g., breach corpuses); SHALL allow password managers and autofill and SHOULD permit paste. Also the basis for noting this reversed older forced-rotation/complexity advice. Illustrative entropy figures were computed independently (95^8 ~ 53 bits; 7776^5 ~ 65 bits) and verified with Python, not taken from the source. Canonical current URL is the 800-63-4 path; the older 800-63-3 (Revision 3) URL is a different, superseded document. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Use Strong Passwords (Secure Our World)
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. federal government consumer guidance (public domain). Read via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-19 (site returns 403 to the default fetcher). Supports: strong passwords should be long (at least 16 characters, longer is stronger), random (a mixed string or a passphrase of 4-7 unrelated words), and unique (a different password for every account); the danger of reuse illustrated by the 'Emma' case, where the same password across bank and email led to account takeover after a company breach appeared online (basis for the reuse/credential-stuffing point); and that a password manager generates, stores, and autofills unique strong passwords so the user remembers only one, plus the reminder to enable MFA on important accounts. Facts synthesized in original prose; no wording reproduced.
